title: Why Normal People Aren’t Using AI Agents
gist: AI agents have roughly 10 million weekly users at OpenAI (Codex plus ChatGPT Work) with similar levels reported at Anthropic (Claude Code, Cowork), against about a billion monthly users each for ChatGPT and Gemini — a rounding error that leaves billions in model training investment uncapitalized. The Browser Company CEO Josh Miller argues 'AI agent' is an industry-invented frame rather than a product category, that labs are shipping capability demos instead of consumer products, and that groupthink (nearly every lab citing the film Her) is narrowing the design space.

insights.claim: OpenAI said last month that its Codex and ChatGPT Work agents collectively have about 10 million weekly users, and people close to Anthropic report its Claude Code and Cowork agents are seeing similar levels of adoption.
insights.speaker: Maxwell Zeff
insights.so_what: The first concrete agent-usage baseline for the two leading labs — the number to track for whether agent monetization is actually inflecting.
insights.locator: Last month, OpenAI said that its Codex and ChatGPT Work agents

insights.claim: Against chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini that each average around a billion monthly active users, agent products at roughly 10 million weekly users amount to basically a rounding error.
insights.speaker: Maxwell Zeff
insights.so_what: A ~100x gap between chat and agent usage means agent revenue assumptions embedded in AI capex narratives are currently unsupported by consumer behavior.
insights.quote: agents amount to basically a rounding error
insights.locator: Compared to chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini

insights.claim: Most consumers use generative AI for simple tasks like looking up information and chatting, while Silicon Valley has spent billions training models capable of far more, making agents the mechanism for capitalizing on that investment only if people actually use them.
insights.speaker: Maxwell Zeff
insights.so_what: The return on frontier training spend is gated on agent adoption specifically — if agents stay niche, the capability overhang stays unmonetized.
insights.locator: That’s a problem for the AI labs

insights.claim: AI insiders report that despite considerable resources poured into building agents, no one has yet created a killer consumer product, leaving open when or whether agents get a ChatGPT-style breakout moment.
insights.speaker: Maxwell Zeff
insights.so_what: Absence of a breakout product after heavy investment is the classic setup for either a sudden category-defining launch or a quiet writedown of the thesis.
insights.locator: This tracks with broader concerns I’ve been hearing among AI insiders

themes.theme: Agents are a technology, not a product

insights.claim: Josh Miller argues that 'AI agent' is an invented frame the industry made up to refer to something internally, not a category consumers want, and that products should be built around outcomes like making a user calm, focused and in flow.
insights.speaker: Maxwell Zeff
insights.so_what: If the category label has no consumer pull, companies marketing 'agents' as the product are mispositioned — value accrues to whoever hides the machinery behind a familiar job-to-be-done.
insights.quote: No one wants AI agents, because AI agents aren't a thing. It is an invented frame made up by our industry to collectively refer to something
insights.locator: Miller’s bigger point is not just that AI agents haven’t caught on yet

insights.claim: The Browser Company's most popular feature ever is a personalized morning briefing in its AI-powered browser Dia — a homepage greeting, a to-do list populated from calendar and email, and small delight items — which is technically powered by an agent the user never sees.
insights.speaker: Maxwell Zeff
insights.so_what: A working existence proof that agent tech succeeds when packaged as an invisible feature — the design pattern to look for in any consumer AI product that actually retains.
insights.locator: Miller has firsthand experience to back up his claims

insights.claim: Miller says he has not heard a single person outside the tech community talk about an agent they use, and argues the industry should pause on its excitement about the frontier and recursive self-improvement.
insights.speaker: Maxwell Zeff
insights.so_what: Anecdotal zero-awareness outside the industry is consistent with the usage data — treat insider enthusiasm as a poor proxy for consumer demand.
insights.quote: I just have not heard a single person outside of the tech community talk about an agent that they use
insights.locator: He says the industry needs to focus on building agent products

insights.claim: Zeff argues that tech companies are shipping the most impressive things their models can do — navigating a website, writing code — rather than products tailored to customer desires, so current agentic products feel more like demos than features.
insights.speaker: Maxwell Zeff
insights.so_what: Capability-led rather than demand-led shipping is a diagnosable product failure; watch for labs hiring consumer product leadership as the signal that it's being corrected.
insights.locator: Miller’s arguments are convenient coming from someone who sells

insights.claim: Zeff notes Miller's argument is conveniently self-serving for someone who sells an AI-powered web browser, while still judging the underlying critique correct.
insights.speaker: Maxwell Zeff
insights.so_what: Discount incentive-aligned commentary, but note the usage numbers independently support the claim — the data, not the source, carries the signal here.
insights.quote: Miller’s arguments are convenient coming from someone who sells an AI-powered web browser.
insights.locator: Miller’s arguments are convenient coming from someone

insights.claim: Miller says that during acquisition talks last summer with leaders at top AI labs, every single lab but one cited the 2013 Spike Jonze film Her as the way they articulated their product vision.
insights.speaker: Maxwell Zeff
insights.so_what: Near-total convergence on one fictional reference means labs are competing to build the same product — the differentiated consumer wins are likely to come from outside the labs.
insights.quote: I think every single lab but one mentioned the movie Her as the way they articulated their vision
insights.locator: Last summer, when The Browser Company was exploring being acquired

insights.claim: Miller attributes the agent adoption failure to industry groupthink, where builders obsessed with the technology share a particular sci-fi vision of how the products should look and feel, producing a lack of diversity of opinions and convictions.
insights.speaker: Maxwell Zeff
insights.so_what: Homogeneous product conviction across well-funded competitors is precisely the condition under which an outsider captures the category.
insights.locator: Miller blames the problem on groupthink in the AI industry

insights.claim: Miller's stated goal is to push founders and product builders beyond OpenAI and Anthropic to question the AI agent narrative and build tools that are joyful, useful and approachable regardless of whether they look like agents.
insights.speaker: Maxwell Zeff
insights.so_what: The framing argues the consumer AI opportunity is open at the application layer even as the model layer consolidates.
insights.quote: Who gives a shit if it looks like an AI agent? No one uses AI agents.
insights.locator: Miller says he hopes his message reaches beyond OpenAI and Anthropic

themes.theme: Miller's credibility and the personal-software trend

insights.claim: Josh Miller's startup The Browser Company built Arc, a web browser with a cult following, and was acquired by Atlassian last year for $610 million; his first company Branch was bought by Facebook in 2014, and he served as the White House's first director of product under President Obama.
insights.speaker: Maxwell Zeff
insights.so_what: A $610 million browser exit into Atlassian gives the critique weight and marks browsers as the contested surface where consumer AI distribution is being fought.

insights.claim: The latest agent trend is letting people build personal software to automate parts of their life — pitch decks, dataset organization and similar tasks — but Zeff argues there is a limited pool of people interested in building their own productivity tools.
insights.speaker: Maxwell Zeff
insights.so_what: The personal-software framing has a small addressable market, so it is unlikely to be the path to the mainstream breakout labs need.
insights.locator: The latest trend with AI agents is giving people the power

insights.claim: Zeff reports personally finding ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork more useful than their predecessors, indicating capability is improving even as consumer pull remains absent.
insights.speaker: Maxwell Zeff
insights.so_what: Separates the capability curve from the adoption curve — the bottleneck is distribution and framing, not model quality.
insights.locator: I’ve personally been using ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork a lot

insights.claim: Within Silicon Valley, agents are already operationally embedded — people are designing payment systems for agents, using them to automate their jobs, and trying to stop them from hacking into other organizations — while most people outside have never touched one.
insights.speaker: Maxwell Zeff
insights.so_what: Agent infrastructure (payments, security) is being built for an insider market — near-term revenue for that infrastructure is B2B and narrow, not consumer scale.
insights.locator: Silicon Valley is already convinced that AI agents are the future
